title: A Flash Sale at Six O'Clock
prompt: A shop has announced a flash sale for 18:00. Design how its servers carry the sale's traffic, and what happens if even more arrives than planned.
facts: One server's measured limit is about 300 requests per second; with recommendations turned off it is about 450, because recommendations are a third of each request's work
The normal peak is 900 requests per second on 6 servers; normally the team keeps each server at or below 65% of its limit, and during a sale it accepts up to 90%
Last year's sale peaked at 2,400 requests per second for 30 minutes; the team plans for the same peak
A new server takes 4 minutes to start and pass its health checks; the autoscaler adds servers after average CPU stays above 65% for 1 minute
The budget allows at most 10 servers at any time
The business allows recommendations to be turned off for up to 1 hour, but would rather keep them

Requirement: up to 2,400 requests per second, no request is refused and no server runs above 90% of its limit; above that, the extra requests are refused at once with "try again in a minute" instead of slowing everyone down
scope: The checkout flow and the database are out of scope; assume the database keeps up

requirements: States the 2,400 per second plan with nothing refused, the 90% ceiling per server, the 10-server budget, and that extra traffic is refused quickly
estimation: Capacity for the chosen design, such as: 10 servers × 300 = 3,000, and 2,400 ÷ 10 = 240 per server, 80% of the limit; or 6 servers with recommendations off, 2,400 ÷ 6 = 400, 89% of 450
The gap if the team waited for the autoscaler: 1 + 4 = 5 minutes on 6 servers (1,800 per second), short by 600 per second, about 180,000 requests in 5 minutes
design: Capacity in place before 18:00, by scaling ahead of time or by turning off recommendations, plus refusing extra requests early at the load balancer
data: The threshold at which requests are refused, such as 90% of the limit across all servers, and which requests are refused first (browsing before checkout)
Clients retry a refused request at most a few times, with backoff and jitter
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: scaling ahead pays for 4 extra servers for the sale; turning off recommendations costs nothing but runs at 89%, close to the ceiling; waiting for the autoscaler leaves a 5-minute gap

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, scale ahead: schedule the server count to rise to the budget of 10 at 17:50, ten minutes before the sale and more than the 4 minutes a server needs. 10 × 300 = 3,000 per second; at 2,400 each server takes 240, 80% of its limit, below 90%, with recommendations on. Above 10 × 270 = 2,700 per second (90%), the load balancer refuses the extra with "try again in a minute", browsing before checkout; phones retry at most twice with backoff and jitter. Trade-off: the shop pays for 4 extra servers for about 40 minutes even if fewer users come.

Design B, degrade ahead: keep 6 servers and turn off recommendations from 17:55 to 18:35, within the 1-hour allowance. Each server's limit becomes 450; at 2,400 each takes 400, 89% of 450, below 90%. Above 6 × 405 = 2,430 per second, the load balancer refuses the extra, and the autoscaler can add up to 4 more servers if traffic stays high. Trade-off: no extra cost, but no recommendations during the sale and only 1% of margin below the ceiling.

assumptions: The sale time is known in advance
Last year's peak is a good guide for this year
reference.design:
The sale time is known, so the shop does not wait for the autoscaler, which would leave a 1 + 4 = 5-minute gap on 6 servers: 1,800 per second against 2,400.
At 17:50 a scheduled action raises the server count to the budget of 10. At 2,400 per second each server takes 240, 80% of its 300 limit, below the 90% ceiling, and recommendations stay on.
The load balancer refuses requests beyond 10 × 270 = 2,700 per second with "try again in a minute", browsing before checkout. Phones retry a refused request at most twice, with backoff and jitter.
If traffic is much higher than planned, recommendations are turned off as a second step, raising the limit to 10 × 450 = 4,500.
alternatives: Turning off recommendations during the sale on 6 servers: 400 per server, 89% of 450; no extra cost, but no recommendations
Rejected: waiting for the autoscaler, because new servers arrive about 5 minutes after the jump, while 600 requests per second have nowhere to go

title: Checkout and a Slow Fraud Check
prompt: Every checkout asks a fraud-check service whether to accept the order. A few times a month that service becomes very slow. Design checkout so that it keeps working when that happens.
facts: About 200 checkouts per second at peak; the shop's servers have 400 workers in total, shared by checkout and every other page
The fraud-check service normally answers within 150 ms; a few times a month it slows down to up to 20 seconds per answer, for up to 10 minutes. When healthy it can check up to 240 orders per second
Requirement: the customer gets an answer within 1 second, either "confirmed" or "received, we will email you" (pending)
Requirement: a slow fraud check must not stop other pages, and the fraud service must never receive more than 1.2 times its normal 200 requests per second

Orders under $50 are 80% of orders; during a fraud-service problem the business accepts confirming them without a check. Orders of $50 or more may stay pending for up to 1 hour and must be checked before they ship
A queue with at-least-once delivery is available (SD 7); checking the same order twice gives the same answer
scope: Payment and shipping are out of scope

requirements: States the 1-second answer (confirmed or pending), that other pages must keep working, the 1.2 times limit on the fraud service, and which orders may skip the check
estimation: Workers held by checkout with a timeout, such as: worst case 300 + 200 + 300 = 800 ms per checkout, 200 × 0.8 = 160 workers of 400; without a timeout, 200 × 20 = 4,000 workers

Or the backlog of pending orders, such as: 200 per second × 600 s = 120,000 orders in a 10-minute slowdown; the spare 40 per second (240 − 200) clears the 24,000 orders of $50 or more in 600 s, within 1 hour
design: A timeout on the fraud call and a fallback when it fails, or a queue between checkout and the fraud check
data: Retries: at most one, with jitter, under a retry budget, or the queue's consumers capped at 240 checks per second
What is saved for a pending order so the check can run later
tradeoffs: Names a trade-off with its condition, such as: confirming small orders without a check accepts some fraud during a slowdown; answering "pending" for every order is safer but less pleasant for customers; a retry helps with a lost answer but adds load

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, call with a timeout and fall back: checkout calls the fraud service with a 300 ms timeout and retries once after a random 0–200 ms wait; retries stop when they pass 10% of calls, so the service sees at most 1.1 times its load, below 1.2. Worst case 300 + 200 + 300 = 800 ms, within 1 second, holding at most 200 × 0.8 = 160 of 400 workers, so other pages keep working. If both tries fail, orders under $50 are confirmed and larger orders are saved as pending and put on a queue: 40 per second × 600 s = 24,000 in a 10-minute slowdown, checked afterwards at 20 per second in about 20 minutes; with retries the service then sees at most 200 + 20 + 20 = 240, 1.2 times its load. Trade-off: about 96,000 small orders may be confirmed unchecked during a slowdown.

Design B, always check from a queue: checkout saves every order as pending with a message (outbox, SD 10) and answers "received, we will email you" in a few milliseconds, holding no worker on the fraud service. Consumers call the fraud service with a 300 ms timeout and at most 240 calls per second, 1.2 times the normal load; a failed check goes back on the queue with backoff. In a 10-minute slowdown 120,000 orders wait; afterwards the spare 40 per second clears the 24,000 orders of $50 or more first, in 600 s, within 1 hour. Trade-off: every customer waits for an email instead of an instant "confirmed", even when the fraud service is healthy.

assumptions: A check can safely be repeated
reference.design:
Checkout calls the fraud service with a 300 ms timeout, two times its normal 150 ms answer. If the call fails, it retries once after a random 0–200 ms wait, and retries stop when they pass 10% of calls, so the fraud service never sees more than 1.1 times its normal load.
Worst case: 300 + 200 + 300 = 800 ms, within the 1-second answer. Checkout holds at most 200 × 0.8 = 160 of the 400 workers, so other pages keep working; without a timeout a slowdown would need 200 × 20 = 4,000.
When both tries fail, orders under $50 are confirmed without a check, as the business allows. Orders of $50 or more are saved as pending and put on a queue; in a 10-minute slowdown that is 40 × 600 = 24,000 orders, checked after it ends at 20 per second, in about 20 minutes, well within 1 hour. Even with the 10% retries, the fraud service then sees at most 200 + 20 + 20 = 240 requests per second, 1.2 times its normal load.
alternatives: Always checking from a queue: no worker waits, but every customer gets "pending" instead of "confirmed"
A circuit breaker that stops calling the fraud service for 30 seconds after many failures, so slow calls are not even tried
Rejected: calling without a timeout, because a 20-second slowdown would need 4,000 workers and stop every page
